results.title: Mobile City Planning Commission Meeting - September 17, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # Mobile City Planning Commission Meeting - September 17, 2026 The Mobile City Planning Commission met on September 17, 2026, to consider a variety of subdivision, rezone, and modification applications. The meeting included public hearings on several items, most notably a major modification at 900 Paper Mill Road in the Africatown overlay district and a rezone application for 5070 Old Shell Road for Food Pack grocery. The commission approved most items with conditions, denied the rezone for Food Pack, and held over other items. ### Consent Calendar - **Agenda Approval**: Approved unanimously. - **Subdivision at 5685 I-10 Industrial Parkway** (Item 1): Held over to October 15, 2026, as requested by the applicant. - **Subdivision at 64 South Dearborn Street** (Item 2): Approved with conditions, including waiver of substandard lot width and area. - **Subdivision at 429 Lincoln Boulevard** (Item 3): Approved with conditions, including waiver of substandard lot area and width. - **Subdivision at 59 and 61 Bradford Avenue and 1311 Azalea Street** (Item 4): Held over to October 15, 2026, at applicant's request, pending resolution of PUD issues. - **Subdivision and sidewalk waiver at 270 Government Boulevard** (Item 8): Approved subdivision with waiver of substandard lot width; sidewalk waiver approved due to no existing sidewalks to connect to. - **Triple application at 53 Foreman Road and 6784/6788 Dickens Ferry Road** (Item 9): Approved subdivision and two modifications, with modifications to corner radius requirements (15-foot radius instead of 25-foot at southwest corner on Foreman and Dickens Ferry). - **Other Business**: Correction to a previously approved subdivision (August 20, 2026) to remove a 25-foot corner radius requirement, approved unanimously. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **Item 5 (900 Paper Mill Road – Major Modification)**: - Ramsey Sprague, President of Mobile Environmental Justice Action Coalition (MeJAC), presented extensive written comments and opposed the application. He argued that the staff report failed to address the Africatown Overlay requirements, including a Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) plan, and that criterion six for approval (noxious or offensive emissions) was not addressed. He noted that ADEM permits already address emissions, dust, odor, etc. He requested a 30-day holdover for proper community engagement, stating that the applicant ignored multiple requests for a neighborhood meeting. - Dr. Joe Womack, retired Marine Major and Africatown native, spoke in opposition. He accused the applicant of clearing land before obtaining permission and criticized lack of community outreach. He emphasized Africatown's historic significance and ongoing revitalization plans (e.g., Lewis Landing, Africatown Blueway). He requested the commission require the applicant to share environmental studies and engage with the community. - Jay Broughton, applicant representative, rebutted that the modifications are within the existing footprint and would reduce visibility and noise by placing materials under a roof. He stated the facility is already operating under existing permits. - **Item 7 (5070 Old Shell Road – Rezone from R1 to B2 for Food Pack grocery)**: - **Supporters**: - Maheen Hijazzi, applicant and owner of Food Pack, spoke in favor, noting 35 years of service, 5,000 petition signatures, and community support. She emphasized that the rezoning would allow the business to continue after losing its lease. - Tim Spifford, architect, presented site plan details and noted that the property was historically labeled commercial but never zoned. He indicated that variances were needed but the site could meet B2 requirements. - Jerry Spiegel, resident, expressed strong support, citing Food Pack's unique offerings and positive neighborhood impact. - Ben Haskassimi, representative of the Iranian community, spoke in favor, highlighting the business's cultural contributions and the need to allow it to continue. - **Opponents**: - Richard Smith, resident of Spring Hill Woods, cited concerns about traffic, stormwater drainage, and the permanent impact of B2 zoning. He noted that the proposed site is not on a thoroughfare and lacks direct frontage. - Kyle Angerson, resident of Country Club Village, opposed the rezoning based on site incompatibility (half-acre lot for a large commercial building), required variances, and potential harm to adjacent homes. He cited drainage, wildlife, and loss of residential character. - Linda St. John, resident of Avalon Street and representative of the Village of Spring Hill, stated opposition, arguing the rezoning violates the Spring Hill Community Master Plan and would set a dangerous precedent. She noted that a residential subdivision was previously approved for the site. - Thomas Myers, resident of Horloester Court, voiced strong opposition, asserting that the application fails to meet objective criteria for rezoning. He highlighted that the property was purchased with knowledge of residential zoning, prior failed commercial attempts, and that the proposed development does not meet basic design requirements. ### Discussion Items - **Item 5 (900 Paper Mill Road)**: Commissioners discussed the applicability of the Africatown Overlay. Staff clarified that the property is within the overlay district but not the safety zone, and that CPTED requirements would be addressed during permitting. A commissioner noted that the condition about fencing was not binding forever; a different fence could be used. The neighborhood meeting requirement applies to planned developments, not modifications of previously approved PUDs. The application was approved with findings of fact A-H. - **Item 7 (5070 Old Shell Road)**: Extensive deliberation occurred. Commissioners discussed the history of the property, including its subdivision label as commercial but actual zoning as R1 since 1967. Staff confirmed that subdivision labels do not dictate zoning. Commissioner Kenny Nichols made a detailed argument against the rezoning, noting: the lot is second-row without direct frontage on Old Shell Road; no commercial development has occurred on similar lots within half a mile in 41 years; 87% of nearby residents opposed; and the applicant's justification (a landlord-tenant dispute) is not sufficient. Commissioner Josh Woods agreed, citing no substantive change in the area to warrant rezoning. The commission voted to deny the rezone recommendation to the City Council. ### Key Outcomes - **Item 1 (5685 I-10 Industrial Parkway)**: Held over to October 15, 2026. - **Items 2, 3, 8**: Subdivisions approved with conditions and waivers. - **Item 4**: Held over to October 15, 2026, in conjunction with Item 10. - **Item 5 (900 Paper Mill Road)**: Major modification **approved** with staff recommendations and findings of fact A through H. (Vote: unanimous) - **Item 6 (East side of Cochrane Causeway)**: Rezone from R1 to I2 **approved** with findings of fact C, D, E, and G. (Vote: unanimous) - **Item 7 (5070 Old Shell Road)**: Rezone from R1 to B2 **denied** by a vote of 9-0 (motion to deny passed). results.title: ERIC ED436094: JALT98 Proceedings. The Proceedings of the JALT Annual International Conference on Language Teaching/Learning & Educational Materials Expo. Focus on the Classroom: Interpretations (24th, Omiya, Saitama, Japan, November 20-23, 1998).
results.creator: ERIC
results.description: This volume includes papers presented at the 1998 Japan Association for Language Teaching Conference. Section 1, "Voices of Experience," includes: "Towards More Use of English in Class by JTEs" (Midori Iwano); "Paperless Portfolios" (Tim Stewart); "Textbook Creation in Reverse Order for Chinese" (Chou Jine Jing); "Career Exploitation Activities for EFL Learners" (Kristin Johannsen); "Lights Up: Drama in the ESL Classroom" (James Welker); "Managing a Successful E-mail Exchange" (Katsumi Ito and Dorothy Zemach); "Preparing for the Possibilities of DVD: Exploiting Language in TV Commercials" (Tim Knowles); "Theme Music Presentation" (Dale Haskell); "Outside Taping for Fluency" (David Kluge and Matthew A. Taylor); "Content and Creation: Student-Generated Textbooks" (Paul Borg and Richard Humphries); "Preparing Students for the Electronic World" (Steve Witt); "Activities for the Independent Learner" (Steve Petrucione and Stephan Ryan); and "Learner Autonomy in Japanese Classrooms: An Exchange of Views" (Leni Dam, David Little, Haruko Katsura, and Richard Smith). Section 2, "Voices of Observation," includes: "Entrapped by Understanding: The Use of the First Language" (Hannah Pillay); "Diagnostic Analysis of Motivational Factors in ESL" (Naoyuki Naganum); "In-Service Training with Japanese Teachers" (Judith Lamie); "Applications of Community Language Learning in Japan" (Tim Greer); "Total Quality Management in the Classroom" (Giles Parker); "Promoting English Use in the EFL Classroom" (Andrew MacNeill, James M. Perren, and Kevin Sullivan); "Discourse-Oriented Pronunciation Activities" (Don Hinkelman and Jerald Halvorsen); "Conversation Teaching Meets Discourse Analysis" (Dominic Cheetham); "Are Japanese Weak at Grammar, Too?" (Mikiya Koari); "Gadgets and Gizmos: Gimmicks or Godsends?" (Chris Pitts and Robert Weschler); "Classroom Activity: Learning Strategies Report" (Fumie Kato); and "Designing and Using Tasks To Promote Optimum Language Development" (Jane Willis). Section 3, "Voices of Interpretation," includes "Autonomy in Foreign Language Learning: From Classroom Practice to Generalizable Theory" (Leni Dam and David Little); "Task Ideas for Junior and Senior High" (Daina Plitkins-Denning); "Looking at Real-World Tasks: Comparing Task-Based and Skill-Based Classroom Instruction" (Peter Robinson, Gregory Strong, and Jennifer Whittle); "The Language Classroom on a Complex Systems Matrix" (Duane Kindt, Naoki Kumai, Paul Lewis, Matthew A. Taylor, and Michael Cholewinski); "Phonological Awareness in EFL Reading Acquisition" (Brett Reynolds); "Japanese Students Academic Literacy in English" (Mayumi Fujioka); "Empowerment and Unionization: Reason, Application and Effect" (Michael Fox, Bill Holden, Farell Cleary, and John McLaughlin); "The Function of Logical Models in Scientific Writing" (Atsuko Yamazaki); "Translating Questionnaires from English into Japanese: Is It Valid?" (Dale Griffee); and "Demystifying the STEP Test" (Laura MacGregor). Section 4, "Voices of Experimentation," includes: "Practicing Action Research" (Lois Scott-Conley, Neil Cowie, Janina Tubby, Richard Hodge, and Schinichi Yokomizo); "Creativity in High School Oral Communication B Classes" (Renee Gauthier Sawazaki); "Questioning Creativity: The CUE Forum on Higher Education" (Jack Kimball, David McMurray, and Brian McVeigh); "Teacher Beliefs and Teacher Development" (Kazuyoshi Sato and Tim Murphy); "Global Education and Language Teacher Training" (Kip Cates, James Kahny, Daniel Kirk, and Lynda-ann Blanchard); "English Language Needs Analysis for EST Students" (Robyn Najar, Guy Kellog, Scott Rogstad, Larraine Sakka, and John Thurman); "CALL: Classroom Interactions" (David Brooks, Joseph Dias, William Bradley, Paul Daniels, and James Wada); "Developing a Self-Access Center" (John E. Ingulsrud, Kate Allen, Miriam Black, Andrew Schaffer, and Patrick Benke); "East Meets West: Approaches to Learner Autonomy" (Jill Robbins); "Measuring Writing Apprehension in Japan" (Steve Cornwell and Sandra Mackay); "The 3D Effect: Combining Course and Self-Assessment" (Alan MacKenzie and Nanci Graves); and "Communication, Context, and Constraint: Working through the Riddles" (Mark A. Clarke). (SM)

results.creator: Law&Crime Network
results.description: NOTE: This is a Death Penalty Case. Donald Hartung, 63, stands trial in Escambia County, Florida for allegedly killing his mother Voncile Smith, 77, and his half-brothers John William Smith, 49, and Richard Thomas Smith, 47. He faces three counts of first-degree premeditated murder. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Escambia County deputies say the crimes happened July 28, 2015, according to an amended arrest report obtained by Law&Crime. Richard Smith, an employee of the Department of Homeland Security, had no-showed worked for a few days, so on deputies checked up on him on July 31. They found no sign of forced entry, but were able to enter through the back with the help of firefighters, and found the three victims dead throughout the home. Each person was under “large piles of clothes,” deputies said. Richard Smith had been shot around his right ear, and had a stab wound to the throat, deputies said. He was found face down in the TV room at the foot of the TV, investigators said. Authorities said he was wearing the same clothes he’d been wearing when pictured leaving work at 6:36 p.m. on July 28. John Smith was found in a sofa on front of a TV. He sustained blunt force trauma to the top of his head, and received a stab wound to the neck, authorities said. As for their mother, she sustained blunt force trauma to the top of her head and received a stab wound to the neck. Authorities said she’d been dragged from a chair into John’s bedroom. According to deputies, Hartung was at the house on the 28th to cook dinner, as usual. He left between 5:30 p.m. and 6:00 pm, he allegedly said, but he denied seeing his brother Richard. A neighbor, however, claimed to see Richard arrive at the residence before Hartung left, investigators said. This witness was not sure of the time, but said it was just before dark because the lights on Hartung’s car was not on, authorities said. Another witness–who was a co-worker’s of Hartung–said that he previously had a conversation with the defendant. In it, the alleged killer said that if anything happened to Voncile Smith, then he would inherit all of her property because he was the oldest son. The mom’s attorney, however, said that she’d kept him out of the will, deputies said. Hartung would’ve been the “potential sole heir” to his family’s estate because there were no other living relatives of the Smith family. The defendant has been called the “Blue Moon Killer” because at the time, the local sheriff described the slayings as “ritualistic” and apparently coincided with a semi-rare blue moon. description: Preface dated London, 1850
Published in 92 parts. Parts are paged continuously; each consists of eight pages, except the last, which has four

First published in 18 weekly installments by Edward Lloyd in The people's periodical and family library, issues 7-24 (21 Nov. 1846 to 20 Mar. 1847); in a greatly expanded version as a penny-part serial in 92 parts (the first four parts issued together) from about 1847-1848; then as a single volume in 1850. The title of the first number ("The string of pearls, or, A sailor's gift : a romance of pecular interest") was revised to "The string of pearls, or, The barber of Fleet Street : a domestic romance" in the course of publication, and a new preface was added

Written by James Malcolm Rymer; cf. Smith, H.R. New light on Sweeney Tood (2002), cited in Mack. Previously attributed to G.A. Macfarren and Thomas P. Prest; also to Edward P. Hingston and to Albert Richard Smith

Illustrated with 89 unsigned wood engravings, one on the first page of each part, except for nos. 1-4, the only numbers issued together, which have only one engraving. Some illustrations are by J. Reading; cf. Mack

Text printed within double fillet border

They found no sign of forced entry, but were able to enter through the back with the help of firefighters, and found the three victims dead throughout the home. Each person was under “large piles of clothes,” deputies said. Richard Smith had been shot around his right ear, and had a stab wound to the throat, deputies said. He was found face down in the TV room at the foot of the TV, investigators said. Authorities said he was wearing the same clothes he’d been wearing when pictured leaving work at 6:36 p.m. on July 28. John Smith was found in a sofa on front of a TV. He sustained blunt force trauma to the top of his head, and received a stab wound to the neck, authorities said. As for their mother, she sustained blunt force trauma to the top of her head and received a stab wound to the neck. Authorities said she’d been dragged from a chair into John’s bedroom. According to deputies, Hartung was at the house on the 28th to cook dinner, as usual. He left between 5:30 p.m. and 6:00 pm, he allegedly said, but he denied seeing his brother Richard. A neighbor, however, claimed to see Richard arrive at the residence before Hartung left, investigators said. This witness was not sure of the time, but said it was just before dark because the lights on Hartung’s car was not on, authorities said. Another witness–who was a co-worker’s of Hartung–said that he previously had a conversation with the defendant. In it, the alleged killer said that if anything happened to Voncile Smith, then he would inherit all of her property because he was the oldest son. The mom’s attorney, however, said that she’d kept him out of the will, deputies said. Hartung would’ve been the “potential sole heir” to his family’s estate because there were no other living relatives of the Smith family. The defendant has been called the “Blue Moon Killer” because at the time, the local sheriff described the slayings as “ritualistic” and apparently coincided with a semi-rare blue moon. results.title: North Kingstown Town Council Meeting Summary — June 22, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # North Kingstown Town Council Meeting — June 22, 2026 The North Kingstown Town Council held a regular meeting on Monday, June 22, 2026, at 7:00 PM in the Town Hall Council Chambers, 80 Boston Neck Road. The council is led by President Gregory A. Mancini, with members Linnea M. Drew, Elizabeth Hill Ross, Dr. Kimberly Ann Page, and Matthew B. McCoy. Notice of the meeting was posted on the Rhode Island Secretary of State's website pursuant to RIGL 42-46-6(c). The docket included special business on the Town Clerk appointment, a 19-item consent calendar (Items 7-25), the Town Manager's report, and new business covering numerous board appointments and a discussion of asphalt odor complaints in the West Davisville area. Record limitations: no meeting minutes were available, and the raw transcript contains no substantive discussion (only the word 'Okay'). As a result, no votes, motions, approvals, or outcomes can be confirmed from the available record. The timestamp associated with the record (2026-06-22 12:00:00 UTC) does not match the 7:00 PM start time listed on the agenda; this summary uses June 22, 2026 as the meeting date, consistent with the agenda. ### Special Business - Item 5: The Town Manager requested the Town Council's Advice and Consent for the appointment of Kerry Rollinson as Town Clerk. - Item 6: The Town Manager was scheduled to swear in Kerry Rollinson as Town Clerk following the council's action. ### Consent Calendar All items on the Consent Agenda (Items 7-25) were considered routine and were scheduled to be enacted by one motion, with items removed upon a request by a council member or citizen. - Item 7: Approval of minutes from the Special Meeting of March 30, 2026, and the Budget Public Hearings of April 13, 2026. - Item 8: Abatement of uncollectable taxes and fees totaling $128,692.57, including write-offs related to a deceased taxpayer and 2014 personal property, motor vehicle, and rescue accounts. - Item 9: Receipt of a donation of a hand-painted scoreboard to be painted on the side of the Field 1 storage shed at Ryan Park by Caitlin Wotherspoon. - Item 10: Award of contract to Envision Technology Advisors, LLC (State MPA #308) for an Information Technology Department Zero Trust True Up in the amount of $12,136.61, funded from the Granicus Video Streaming Software Account. - Item 11: Award of contract to Envision Technology Advisors (State MPA #308, Award #3806678) for Information Technology Managed Services Provider services in the amount of $156,600.00, funded from the FY2027 IT Maintenance Account. - Item 12: Award of a contract extension to CAI Technologies for Assessor's Parcel and Zoning Layer Maintenance and Web Geographic Information System Application, at various prices, funded from the Annual Miscellaneous Software License Account. - Item 13: Award of contract to BEI Holdings, dba Business Electronics, for one Detective Interview Room Recording System for the Police Department in the amount of $14,520.00, funded from the Police Capital Outlay Account. - Item 14: Approval of a sole source purchase from Motorola Solutions, Inc. of seven portable radios with accessories for the Police Department in the amount of $48,582.87 (State MPA #395), funded from the Police Capital Outlay Account. - Item 15: Award of a sole source purchase to Advanced Weighing Systems for an upgrade to the Department of Public Works Transfer Station scale computer software in the amount of $10,670.00, funded from the FY2026 Transfer Station Contractual Services Account. - Item 16: Approval of a purchase from Minuteman Security & Life Safety for Department of Senior Services security camera system upgrades and installation of an additional camera in the amount of $15,622.00 (State MPA #419), funded from the Capital Outlay Account. - Item 17: New entertainment license for Cocumscussoc Association, dba Smith's Castle, 55 Richard Smith Drive, for a live concert on the grounds of Smith's Castle on July 19, 2026 (rain date Sunday, August 2, 2026). - Item 18: New exhibition license (no vendors) for RI Elder Info, 70 Romano Vineyard Way, Suite 111, for the 7th Annual Calling All Veterans Day, a Veteran and Community Senior Resource Fair, on August 15, 2026 (rain date August 22, 2026). - Item 19: New fireworks permit for Plum Beach Club, 224 Plum Beach Road, Saunderstown, for a fireworks display on June 26, 2026 (rain date July 11, 2026). - Item 20: New fireworks permit for Quidnessett Country Club, 950 North Quidnessett Road, for a fireworks display on Tuesday, July 4, 2026, as stated in the agenda. - Item 21: Peddler license renewal for Keystone Novelties Distributors LLC to sell sparklers and novelty devices under a tent at 6653 Post Road. - Item 22: Peddler license renewal for Keystone Novelties Distributors LLC to sell sparklers and novelty devices under a tent at 4020 Quaker Lane. - Item 23: Victualling license renewal for Cloud Donuts, Inc., 6689 Post Road. - Item 24: Authorization for the Town Manager to sign and ratify a Memorandum of Understanding regarding the Town of North Kingstown's Remote Net Metering Agreement between the Town and the North Kingstown School Committee. - Item 25: First reading of an amendment to Section 2-1, entitled 'Competitive Bidding Required.' ### Public Comments & Testimony - The agenda provided a Public Comment period with a three-minute speaking limit, but no public testimony appears in the available transcript. ### Reports - Item 26: Report by the Town Manager, described in the agenda as including the Town Manager's regular update on Quonset-related issues. ### Discussion Items - Item 27: Asset Management Commission appointments: one School Committee Representative to July 1, 2029; one Technical Representative to July 1, 2029; three At-Large Representatives to July 1, 2029; and one At-Large Representative to July 1, 2027 to fill an unexpired term. Applications were attached from James Halley, Stephen Raymond, John Pyne, Lisa Bowe, and Andrew Sullivan. - Item 28: Building Code Board of Appeals: one member to July 1, 2031. - Item 29: Information Technology Advisory Committee: one Alternate At-Large Member to March 1, 2029. - Item 30: Leisure Services Advisory Committee: three members to July 1, 2029. Applications were attached from Keith Finck and Jeffrey Smith. - Item 31: Personnel Board: one member to March 1, 2029. - Item 32: Planning Commission: one member to July 1, 2032. An application was attached from Richard Lipsitz. - Item 33: Probate Judge to July 1, 2027. An application was attached from Brian Fielding. - Item 34: Veteran's Memorial Scholarship Fund Committee: two members to July 1, 2027. - Item 35: Wickford Village Design Guidelines Committee: one Alternate Business Property Owner to December 31, 2027. - Item 36: Councilor Beth Hill Ross requested discussion concerning Public Comment. - Item 37: Council President Mancini requested discussion and possible action regarding numerous complaints received by both the Town of North Kingstown and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management about the unacceptable asphalt smell in the West Davisville area. - Item 38: Correspondence. ### Key Outcomes - No decisions, votes, or actions can be confirmed from the available record. The raw transcript contains no substantive content, and no minutes were provided, so the council's disposition of the Town Clerk appointment, the consent calendar, the Town Manager's report, the appointments, or the asphalt odor discussion is not documented.

results.creator: CIA Reading Room
results.description: STAT Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2012/12/11 CIA-RDP89 BO 1354 R000400480031-2 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2012/12/11 CIA-RDP89 BO 1354 R000400480031-2 Declassified in Part - Sanitized Copy Approved for Release 2012/12/11: CIA-RDP89B01354R000400480031-2 Director of Central intelligence Security Committee Computer Security Subcommittee 1. The one hundred and seventy-fifth meeting of the Computer Security Subcommittee was convened on 15 October 1985 at the meeting: The following persons attended the Executive Secretary Mrs. Karen Deneroff, Dept. of State Mr. Norman Clark, Navy Mr. Richard Smith, Navy Major Jack Freeman, Army Mr. David Schenken, US Secret Service CIA Mr. Paul Fitzgerald, FBI NSA Mr. Robert Graytoc , Dept. of Justice Mr. Michael Bernott, Air Force SECOM IC Staff/IHC IC Staff/IHC 2. The minutes of the previous minutes were reviewed. It was noted that Mr. Graytock was incorrectly listed as being from the Dept. of Treasury. He is, in fact, the member from the Dept. of Justice. A number of corrections and updates to the membership list were also received. The corrected membership list is attached. 3. The first discussion dealt with the issue of the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for facility approvals. Specifically, we discussed the paper, "Proposed Changes and Modifications to DCID 1/16, Computer Security Manual". Rather than dealing with the details of the MOU and the process for achieving joint accreditation of facilities, the discussion centered about the discrepancies between the formally defined accreditation process and how systems actually get "on the air" under current practice. The distinctions between initial operational approval and full certification and accreditation were discussed at length. Since the formally defined process is involved and lengthy, an informal process has evolved by which someone well below the DAA can grant an interim operational approval for a system, thus allowing it to operate without full accreditation. Since the interim approval process is informal, the "interim" status may, in fact, be indefinite. Thus, the result of this process is that a number of systems are currently operating which have never been, and never will be, formally accredited. It was argued that the currently defined accreditation process does not work; many systems are operating with only interim approval. On the other hand, if the defined process is strictly enforced, then needed operational capability will not be available due to the delays the process creates. Thus, the argument was for a well-defined and enforceable process for accreditation which recognizes the need for, and accomodates and regulates, the interim approval process. The membership next discussed. mechanisms for regulating and limiting the interim status. Mr.Clark and agreed to prepare a strawman description of the interim approval process. 'i'he next topic aiscussea was the worK on the rk, security Guidelines, which has been contracted to the National Bureau of Standards. It was noted that there were three deliverables under this effort, the first of which was a user's brochure. A draft of this deliverable was distributed. The schedule was also reviewed. STAT 5. The status of the funding for R&D tasks was reviewed. There are essentially no funds for fy86. Apparently, the view is that the SECOM should provide seed money for selected projects which need a start, but that they should not be in the business of providing continuing funding of R&D programs. Long-term funding, it is felt, should be provided by a department or agency; the proper role of the SECOM is to fund new initiatives. Along a similar vein, reported, in response to a previous inquery, that the Computer Security Center's R&D organization (i.e., C3) could respond to tasking from both the CSS and the civil agencies. However, it was noted that the Center has yet to receive R&D requirements from the civil agencies. The conclusion is that the CSS' perceived needs for Intel community computer security R&D can be communicated to the National Computer Security Center. It was felt that was STAT the proper channel through which to communicate such requirements. 6. Miscellaneous items: - reported that the 2nd Annual Computer Security Report is now being compiled by the NTISSC. Good cooperation is being experienced from the various participating agencies. - Major Freeman reviewed some of the work on DoDD 5200.28 and 5200.28M. Current drafts include requirements from the Trusted Computer System Evaluation Criteria. - John Lane will be leaving ASD(C3I), and will be going to the Department of Justice. - Dave Jones has left the Department of Energy, joining the National Computer Security Center. He will be replaced by Mr. Leon Breault (sp ?). 7. results.title: Clusters in a cold climate : innovation dynamics in a diverse economy
results.creator: Innovation Systems Research Network. Conference (5th : 2003 : Ottawa, Ont.)
description: x, 228 pages : 24 cm

"As Canada emerges from the recent economic downturn, firms in industrial clusters face a series of unique challenges. From established clusters in auto parts and wine, to emerging clusters in biotechnology, photonics and multimedia, firms must adapt to rapidly changing demand and cost conditions, cope with increased competition at home and abroad, and finance an accelerating pace of innovation. The papers in this volume examine how firms in eight clusters are meeting these challenges by accessing resources and markets, managing economic uncertainty, and adapting to market changes. Representing the latest research findings from members of the Innovation Systems Research Network, the papers highlight a number of key themes: the contribution of both local and global sources of knowledge to innovation within the clusters, the powerful draw of external markets that can act as the primary stimulus to innovative behaviour, the interaction between key elements of the research infrastructure and innovative firms, and the complex, but essential, influence of public policy on cluster dynamics."--BOOK JACKET
Papers presented at the 5th Annual Conference of the Innovation Systems Research Network, held in Ottawa, Ont., May 1-2, 2003
Includes bibliographical references

Introduction: clusters in a cold climate / David A. Wolfe and Matthew Lucas -- Shifting gears: restructuring and innovation in the Ontario automotive parts industry / Susan Fitzgibbon [and others] -- Learning, innovation and cluster growth: a study of two inherited organizations in the Niagara Peninsula wine cluster / Lynn K. Mytelka and Haeli Goertzen -- Biotechnology companies and clustering in Nova Scotia / Philip Rosson and Carolan McLarney -- The biotechnology cluster in Vancouver / J. results.title: North Kingstown Town Council Meeting Summary — June 22, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # North Kingstown Town Council Meeting — June 22, 2026 The North Kingstown Town Council held a regular meeting on Monday, June 22, 2026, at 7:00 PM in the Town Hall Council Chambers, 80 Boston Neck Road. The council is led by President Gregory A. Mancini, with members Linnea M. Drew, Elizabeth Hill Ross, Dr. Kimberly Ann Page, and Matthew B. McCoy. Notice of the meeting was posted on the Rhode Island Secretary of State's website pursuant to RIGL 42-46-6(c). The docket included special business on the Town Clerk appointment, a 19-item consent calendar (Items 7-25), the Town Manager's report, and new business covering numerous board appointments and a discussion of asphalt odor complaints in the West Davisville area. Record limitations: no meeting minutes were available, and the raw transcript contains no substantive discussion (only the word 'Okay'). As a result, no votes, motions, approvals, or outcomes can be confirmed from the available record. The timestamp associated with the record (2026-06-22 12:00:00 UTC) does not match the 7:00 PM start time listed on the agenda; this summary uses June 22, 2026 as the meeting date, consistent with the agenda. ### Special Business - Item 5: The Town Manager requested the Town Council's Advice and Consent for the appointment of Kerry Rollinson as Town Clerk. - Item 6: The Town Manager was scheduled to swear in Kerry Rollinson as Town Clerk following the council's action. ### Consent Calendar All items on the Consent Agenda (Items 7-25) were considered routine and were scheduled to be enacted by one motion, with items removed upon a request by a council member or citizen. - Item 7: Approval of minutes from the Special Meeting of March 30, 2026, and the Budget Public Hearings of April 13, 2026. - Item 8: Abatement of uncollectable taxes and fees totaling $128,692.57, including write-offs related to a deceased taxpayer and 2014 personal property, motor vehicle, and rescue accounts. - Item 9: Receipt of a donation of a hand-painted scoreboard to be painted on the side of the Field 1 storage shed at Ryan Park by Caitlin Wotherspoon. - Item 10: Award of contract to Envision Technology Advisors, LLC (State MPA #308) for an Information Technology Department Zero Trust True Up in the amount of $12,136.61, funded from the Granicus Video Streaming Software Account. - Item 11: Award of contract to Envision Technology Advisors (State MPA #308, Award #3806678) for Information Technology Managed Services Provider services in the amount of $156,600.00, funded from the FY2027 IT Maintenance Account. - Item 12: Award of a contract extension to CAI Technologies for Assessor's Parcel and Zoning Layer Maintenance and Web Geographic Information System Application, at various prices, funded from the Annual Miscellaneous Software License Account. - Item 13: Award of contract to BEI Holdings, dba Business Electronics, for one Detective Interview Room Recording System for the Police Department in the amount of $14,520.00, funded from the Police Capital Outlay Account. - Item 14: Approval of a sole source purchase from Motorola Solutions, Inc. of seven portable radios with accessories for the Police Department in the amount of $48,582.87 (State MPA #395), funded from the Police Capital Outlay Account. - Item 15: Award of a sole source purchase to Advanced Weighing Systems for an upgrade to the Department of Public Works Transfer Station scale computer software in the amount of $10,670.00, funded from the FY2026 Transfer Station Contractual Services Account. - Item 16: Approval of a purchase from Minuteman Security & Life Safety for Department of Senior Services security camera system upgrades and installation of an additional camera in the amount of $15,622.00 (State MPA #419), funded from the Capital Outlay Account. - Item 17: New entertainment license for Cocumscussoc Association, dba Smith's Castle, 55 Richard Smith Drive, for a live concert on the grounds of Smith's Castle on July 19, 2026 (rain date Sunday, August 2, 2026). - Item 18: New exhibition license (no vendors) for RI Elder Info, 70 Romano Vineyard Way, Suite 111, for the 7th Annual Calling All Veterans Day, a Veteran and Community Senior Resource Fair, on August 15, 2026 (rain date August 22, 2026). - Item 19: New fireworks permit for Plum Beach Club, 224 Plum Beach Road, Saunderstown, for a fireworks display on June 26, 2026 (rain date July 11, 2026). - Item 20: New fireworks permit for Quidnessett Country Club, 950 North Quidnessett Road, for a fireworks display on Tuesday, July 4, 2026, as stated in the agenda. - Item 21: Peddler license renewal for Keystone Novelties Distributors LLC to sell sparklers and novelty devices under a tent at 6653 Post Road. - Item 22: Peddler license renewal for Keystone Novelties Distributors LLC to sell sparklers and novelty devices under a tent at 4020 Quaker Lane. - Item 23: Victualling license renewal for Cloud Donuts, Inc., 6689 Post Road. - Item 24: Authorization for the Town Manager to sign and ratify a Memorandum of Understanding regarding the Town of North Kingstown's Remote Net Metering Agreement between the Town and the North Kingstown School Committee. - Item 25: First reading of an amendment to Section 2-1, entitled 'Competitive Bidding Required.' ### Public Comments & Testimony - The agenda provided a Public Comment period with a three-minute speaking limit, but no public testimony appears in the available transcript. ### Reports - Item 26: Report by the Town Manager, described in the agenda as including the Town Manager's regular update on Quonset-related issues. ### Discussion Items - Item 27: Asset Management Commission appointments: one School Committee Representative to July 1, 2029; one Technical Representative to July 1, 2029; three At-Large Representatives to July 1, 2029; and one At-Large Representative to July 1, 2027 to fill an unexpired term. Applications were attached from James Halley, Stephen Raymond, John Pyne, Lisa Bowe, and Andrew Sullivan. - Item 28: Building Code Board of Appeals: one member to July 1, 2031. - Item 29: Information Technology Advisory Committee: one Alternate At-Large Member to March 1, 2029. - Item 30: Leisure Services Advisory Committee: three members to July 1, 2029. Applications were attached from Keith Finck and Jeffrey Smith. - Item 31: Personnel Board: one member to March 1, 2029. - Item 32: Planning Commission: one member to July 1, 2032. An application was attached from Richard Lipsitz. - Item 33: Probate Judge to July 1, 2027. An application was attached from Brian Fielding. - Item 34: Veteran's Memorial Scholarship Fund Committee: two members to July 1, 2027. - Item 35: Wickford Village Design Guidelines Committee: one Alternate Business Property Owner to December 31, 2027. - Item 36: Councilor Beth Hill Ross requested discussion concerning Public Comment. - Item 37: Council President Mancini requested discussion and possible action regarding numerous complaints received by both the Town of North Kingstown and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management about the unacceptable asphalt smell in the West Davisville area. - Item 38: Correspondence. ### Key Outcomes - No decisions, votes, or actions can be confirmed from the available record. The raw transcript contains no substantive content, and no minutes were provided, so the council's disposition of the Town Clerk appointment, the consent calendar, the Town Manager's report, the appointments, or the asphalt odor discussion is not documented.

results.title: Donald Hartung Trial Day 1 - Christine Rollins - Fmr Crime Scene Tech Part 2
results.creator: Law&Crime Network
results.description: NOTE: This is a Death Penalty Case. Donald Hartung, 63, stands trial in Escambia County, Florida for allegedly killing his mother Voncile Smith, 77, and his half-brothers John William Smith, 49, and Richard Thomas Smith, 47. He faces three counts of first-degree premeditated murder. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Escambia County deputies say the crimes happened July 28, 2015, according to an amended arrest report obtained by Law&Crime. Richard Smith, an employee of the Department of Homeland Security, had no-showed worked for a few days, so on deputies checked up on him on July 31. They found no sign of forced entry, but were able to enter through the back with the help of firefighters, and found the three victims dead throughout the home. Each person was under “large piles of clothes,” deputies said. Richard Smith had been shot around his right ear, and had a stab wound to the throat, deputies said. He was found face down in the TV room at the foot of the TV, investigators said. Authorities said he was wearing the same clothes he’d been wearing when pictured leaving work at 6:36 p.m. on July 28. John Smith was found in a sofa on front of a TV. He sustained blunt force trauma to the top of his head, and received a stab wound to the neck, authorities said. As for their mother, she sustained blunt force trauma to the top of her head and received a stab wound to the neck. Authorities said she’d been dragged from a chair into John’s bedroom. According to deputies, Hartung was at the house on the 28th to cook dinner, as usual. He left between 5:30 p.m. and 6:00 pm, he allegedly said, but he denied seeing his brother Richard. A neighbor, however, claimed to see Richard arrive at the residence before Hartung left, investigators said. This witness was not sure of the time, but said it was just before dark because the lights on Hartung’s car was not on, authorities said. Another witness–who was a co-worker’s of Hartung–said that he previously had a conversation with the defendant. In it, the alleged killer said that if anything happened to Voncile Smith, then he would inherit all of her property because he was the oldest son. The mom’s attorney, however, said that she’d kept him out of the will, deputies said. Hartung would’ve been the “potential sole heir” to his family’s estate because there were no other living relatives of the Smith family. The defendant has been called the “Blue Moon Killer” because at the time, the local sheriff described the slayings as “ritualistic” and apparently coincided with a semi-rare blue moon. According to deputies, Hartung was at the house on the 28th to cook dinner, as usual. He left between 5:30 p.m. and 6:00 pm, he allegedly said, but he denied seeing his brother Richard. A neighbor, however, claimed to see Richard arrive at the residence before Hartung left, investigators said. This witness was not sure of the time, but said it was just before dark because the lights on Hartung’s car was not on, authorities said. Another witness–who was a co-worker’s of Hartung–said that he previously had a conversation with the defendant. In it, the alleged killer said that if anything happened to Voncile Smith, then he would inherit all of her property because he was the oldest son. The mom’s attorney, however, said that she’d kept him out of the will, deputies said. Hartung would’ve been the “potential sole heir” to his family’s estate because there were no other living relatives of the Smith family. The defendant has been called the “Blue Moon Killer” because at the time, the local sheriff described the slayings as “ritualistic” and apparently coincided with a semi-rare blue moon. results.title: East Providence City Council Meeting - July 7, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # East Providence City Council Meeting - July 7, 2026 This regular meeting of the East Providence City Council covered a range of topics including sewer abatements, proclamations, a public hearing and final passage of an ordinance appropriating $340,035 for softball field improvements, approvals of licenses, communications from the SBA, and various council member items regarding infrastructure, public safety, and community events. The meeting concluded with several resolutions and adjournment. ### Consent Calendar - **Sewer Charge Abatement:** Approved $378.58 abatement for a water break related to a bathroom pipe, recommended by the Department of Public Works. Motion by Councilman Bogarty, seconded by Councilman Lawson. Unanimous. - **Consent Calendar Items:** Council journals (June 16, 2026), new addresses (156 Amarillo St, 9 Regent Drive), cancellations and abatements ($6,647.24). Motion by Councilwoman Sousa, seconded by Councilman Fogerty. Unanimous. - **Licenses:** Bundled items 1-10 (entertainment, alcohol, new business licenses for East Providence Fuel, etc.) approved with a motion by Councilman Lawson and second by Councilwoman Sousa. Unanimous. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **Softball Field Improvements (Public Hearing):** Multiple speakers expressed support for lighting and improvements at Amaral Field. - Richard Hogan (President of East Providence Central Little League) detailed the league's growth (200-250 players, 80 volunteers), the lack of lights causing scheduling difficulties, and the need for equity with baseball fields. He noted that the junior/senior division girls will represent Rhode Island in Pennsylvania. - Christina O'Reilly (coach and parent) explained that without lights, older girls (13-15) cannot practice after school, limiting seasons. She cited a Women's Sports Foundation study that girls drop out at twice the rate of boys by age 14. - Jonathan McGowan (Vice President of East Providence Central Little League) highlighted the growth from 76 players to nearly 100 in one year and urged support. - A resident (parent of six, five girls) spoke in favor, showing the growth in divisions (coach pitch, minors, majors, juniors/seniors) and the team's success in all-stars. - **Additional Hours for Fuel Sales (Public Hearing):** No public speakers for or against. The applicant (Nicholas Lambrose, attorney) explained the need for 24-hour fuel sales at the new East Providence Fuels (formerly Exxon). The council clarified that during 1 a.m. to 6 a.m., only fuel sales would occur, not repairs. Approved with that condition. ### Discussion Items - **Council President Rodrigues - World Cup Recognition:** Rodrigues thanked the Scottish "Tartan Army" for their positive impact, including a $10,000 donation to Hasbro Children's Hospital and general goodwill. He wore a kilt in tribute. - **Councilman Lawson - Budget Requests:** Proposed adding a DPW rodent/pest control specialist (like Cranston and Warwick), improvements to Oldham (city-owned building), and reviewing school department head teaching loads. The administration acknowledged and will consider. - **Councilman Lawson - Parking for Crescent Park Events:** With construction reducing parking, he suggested shuttles from off-site lots, local traffic restrictions, and using private lots. Councilwoman Sousa noted that a shuttle was used for the recent block party and should be replicated. The administration will coordinate. - **Councilman Lawson - Willet Avenue Traffic Redesign:** He criticized the road diet and yield sign configuration, stating residents feel ignored. Administration explained the redesign was based on resident feedback and engineering standards to reduce speeding, with no major accidents reported. Lawson disagreed, calling the road diet unsafe. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Veterans Hero Banners:** Out of 108 orders, 86 paid; banners have been ordered and will be installed by August on Roger Williams Ave, Bullocks Point Ave, and Pawtucket Ave (pending confirmation). A digital payment option will be implemented for future orders. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Pedestrian Crosswalks on Warren Avenue:** Asked for timeline on crosswalk signals at Lions Ave and 7th St. Administration will check with DPW director Dan. Sousa stressed safety issues for children crossing to bus stops. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Speed Monitoring on Burgess Avenue:** Requested traffic study and calming measures. Council Vice President Rigo recommended contacting police chief for a traffic study first. Administration will request study from chief. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Street Light Adjustment:** Requested brighter lighting in dark neighborhoods, especially near parks. Administration noted balance between safety, energy cost, and bulb life, and will review specific locations. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Trash Receptacles at Parks and Bus Stops:** Requested more trash cans at parks (e.g., Martello Park) and bus stops. Administration stated RIPTA is responsible for bus stops, but will coordinate; they noted a carry-in/carry-out policy and capacity limits for 44 parks. - **Council Vice President Rigo - ADU Tax Stabilization:** Second passage of ordinance amending tax stabilization for qualified businesses to include accessory dwelling units (ADUs), for owner-occupied properties with homestead exemption only. Rigo explained it helps with housing crisis without building on new land. Passed 4-1. - **Resolutions:** - **Window Replacement at City Hall:** Contract with Red Oak Remodeling for $482,545 for exterior windows, previously discussed. Unanimous. - **Easement for Police Substation:** Granting easement to Narragansett Electric for power to police substation at Pierce Field, previously discussed. Unanimous. - **Furniture for Community Center:** Authorizing purchase of furniture, fixtures, and equipment from W.B. Mason for $172,539.75, using previously allocated funds (ARPA/CPF grant). Unanimous. ### Key Outcomes - **Sewer Abatement Approved** Unanimous. - **Consent Calendar and Licenses Approved** Unanimous. - **Pierce Softball Field Improvements Ordinance Approved** Unanimously (second passage, public hearing held). The $340,035 allocation covers lights, paved parking, walkways, guardrails, and will be contracted with New School Lighting. - **Additional Hours for Fuel Sales Approved** (with condition of no repairs between 1 a.m. and 6 a.m.) Unanimous. - **ADU Tax Stabilization Ordinance Approved** 4-1. - **Resolutions for City Hall Windows, Easement, and Community Center Furniture Approved** Unanimously. - **Veterans Hero Banners:** Expected installation by August. - **Willet Avenue Traffic Pattern:** Administration stands by redesign; further complaints will be brought back. - **Various Council Requests:** Administration will follow up on parking, speed monitoring, crosswalks, street lights, and trash receptacles.

results.title: Marcandier ERV Projet 2015
results.creator: René Viénet
results.description: Roch Marcandier HISTOIRE DES HOMMES DE PROYE ou Les Crimes du Comité de Surveillance et des buveurs de sang, dénoncés à tous les peuples.  Il subsiste peu d’ exemplaires originaux de ce pamphlet : selon WorldCat, à la bibliothèque de la Fondation Thiers à Paris et un autre à la BNF. Egalement à la British Library, la National Library of Scotland, Roger Williams U. Library,  U. of  Leeds Library.  En ligne, sous   Internet Archive , un scan complet  - l'exemplaire de la Newberrys - est disponible : https://archive.org/details/histoiredeshomme00marc/page/3/mode/1up La présente édition en ligne reprend, en caractère Didot, l'originale de 1792 de Roch Marcandier (66 pages, Imprimerie des Droits de l'Homme) de notre exemplaire original, acheté chez un libraire parisien.  L'orthographe et la ponctuation en ont été respectées, en intégrant dans le corps du texte [signalées entre crochets, en caractère maigre] les notes en bas de page de l'auteur.   La pagination de cette version mise en ligne est aberrante compte-tenu d’un certain nombre de pages à venir dans l’édition  libraire. Le texte original diffère légèrement de la réédition en 1835 par Buchez & Roux dans le 18e tome (page 181 à 215) de leur " Histoire parlementaire de la Révolution française ... " (40 volumes, Paris, Paulin, 1834-1838).  Le fichier photographique de notre exemplaire original, plus clair que celui de la Newberrys, sera également mis en ligne - sur ce même site Internet Archive - en attendant une édition définitive libraire, avec notre introduction mise à jour. Dans cette introduction, dont une première version est mise en ligne séparément sous   Internet Archive , il est expliqué pourquoi  certains § sont surlignés en jaune  : il s’agît des passages que L-S. Mercier —  dans son  Nouveau Paris —  a dérobé à Marcandier,  sans jamais le citer, ni même mentionner son exécution. Bien évidemment, aucun des spécialistes de Mercier ne s’en est aperçu, ni malheureusement aucun des spécialistes (plus rares) de Roch Marcandier  … Ces  trois mises en ligne (la numérisation de l’édition originale, sa reprise en typographie, notre introduction provisoire) sont réalisées en octobre 2021, à l’occasion d’un débat sur Marie-Olympe de Gouges,  et les Massacres de septembre. René Viénet

results.title: American poetry of the seventeenth century
results.creator: None
description: xxxvi, 541 pages ; 23 cm

"Reissued in response to demand, this definitive anthology of colonial American poetry is made available in a classroom edition, with annotatory emendations reflecting recent scholarship. The book presents 250 representative poems—fifty-nine printed here for the first time—accompanied by Professor Meserole's illuminating introduction, notes, glosses, comments, and catalogue of sources.The poets represented range from well-known writers such as Anne Bradstreet, Edward Taylor, and Michael Wigglesworth to personages not known primarily for their poetry—including Cotton Mather, Governor William Bradford, Roger Williams, and Captain John Smith—to the less famous such as schoolteacher Sarah Kemble Knight, lawyer Richard Chamberlain, and former indentured servant George Alsop. The poetry here offers a wide range of expression, including love lyrics, religious meditation, political satire, elegies, and personal narratives." --Publisher's Description
Previously published as: Seventeenth-century American poetry
Includes bibliographical references (pages 517-522) and index

results.title: Cranston City Council Budget Hearing for FY2026-2027 - April 16, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # Cranston City Council Finance Committee Budget Hearing - April 16, 2026 The Cranston City Council Finance Committee held a public hearing on the proposed FY2026-2027 budget on April 16, 2026, starting at approximately 7:39 PM and adjourning at 11:49 PM. The meeting focused on the mayor's proposed 7.44% tax levy increase and the financial challenges facing the city, particularly the school department. The committee heard testimony from school committee members, citizens, and representatives from police, fire, schools, and other departments. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **School Committee Vice Chair Anthony Melillo** (33 Harvard Street) presented "myths vs facts," stating that Cranston Public Schools reduced staff by 95 positions over the past four years (not added 100), and that over the last six years the city allocation increased by only about $1 million annually on average, which has not kept pace with rising costs. He emphasized shared responsibility for the budget challenges. - **School Committee Member Catherine Crowley** (Ward 6) explained the school department's structural deficit, noting that the mayor's proposed $1.5 million increase is insufficient. She warned that cuts would lower education quality and deter new teachers. - **School Committee Member Keith Catone** (61 Windsor Road) challenged claims of deficits, stating the school department only recorded a deficit in FY25, while FY24, 23, and 22 had surpluses. He argued that the city budget has been balanced "on the backs of the schools" and that transparency is needed to build public trust. - **Resident Valerie (last name unclear)** stated that taxpayers have "nothing left to give" and urged the council to find budget cuts rather than increase taxes, emphasizing the strain on seniors and families. - **Councilman Steven Steikos** (37 Ferncrest Avenue) observed that school funding increased only 4.3% total from 2024 to 2027, while fire and police funding increased 15.6% and 12.5% respectively. He also noted an $852,000 cash balance in the charter school account and suggested reviewing tax breaks for veterans and elderly. - **Resident Stephen Fryers** (107 Garden Hills Drive) said the budget problem is a "failure in local government" due to over-reliance on one-time federal ARPA funds. He recommended spending cuts and not going above an 8% tax rate effect. - **School Committee Member Anna Madeiris** (21 Bridgeton Court) shared positive stories of student achievements and urged full funding for schools, warning that deteriorating buildings and large class sizes hurt students. - **School Committee Chair Dominic Fusco** (no address provided) noted that Cranston spends $19,950 per student, well below the state average of $22,800. He said the school department has "no choice now but to close schools, increase class sizes, cut programs." - **Local 1363 President Jonathan Francis** (35 Fifth Avenue) defended the fire department, stating that a fifth rescue was added after 40 years and that the department faces 12 vacancies. He said minimum manning of 43 firefighters per shift falls short of the national standard. - **Seventh grader Sally Finkel** (55 Roger Williams Circle) asked to fully fund schools to preserve middle school sports, which she said give students motivation and community. ### Discussion Items #### Police Department Budget (Chief Winquist, Director Strom) - Proposed budget: $33 million. The chief described the budget as "bare bones" and stated that overtime budget of $2.2 million is aligned with historical averages. There are six vacancies; the department had to reduce vehicle purchases from eight to six due to cuts. - Revenue projections were adjusted downward because previous years were overestimated (e.g., police detail car revenues were underperforming). - The department is in contract negotiations; a contingency line item of $700,000 is included for potential contract costs. - Council members questioned gas/oil budget adequacy ($12,500 increase) and the need for more police vehicles given high mileage. The acting director noted oil prices are speculative but assumed the Middle East conflict would not persist. #### Animal Control (Chief Winquist) - The shelter is handling more animals due to economic pressures; budget increase of $10,000 for care. Revenue from impound fees is projected lower due to conservative estimates. - The department uses social media to promote adoptions; average stay is 4-6 weeks. #### Harbor Master - No current harbor master since previous one passed away. The city still collects mooring fees (~$3,500 last year without a harbor master). The council discussed whether to reinstate the position (stipend $3,500) or have police handle duties, but noted the net revenue gain is small. #### School Department Budget (Superintendent Massey, CFO Balducci) - The school department requested $4.2 million new city funding to meet contractual obligations (salary and benefits). The mayor proposed $1.5 million. The state aid increase is estimated at $2 million, but when accounting for a $241,000 reduction in non-public transportation support, net new state money is about $1.8 million. - The school department has a budget savings gap of approximately $3 million (assumes $4 million city ask). If only $1.5 million is provided, the gap grows to $2.5 million. - Cranston Public Schools has cut 95 staff over the last six years and laid off 40 teachers this year; about 12 will likely not be called back. Class sizes are already at contractual limits, and further cuts will increase class sizes and reduce services. - The district spends $19,950 per student, well below the state average. Inflation since 2009 is 56-58%, but city funding only increased 18% over the same period. - Health insurance costs have risen 15% and 10% in the last two years; the district is self-insured and part of a collaborative. A cumulative deficit of $9 million exists, but a new pharmacy contract is expected to generate $4.5 million annually to reduce it. - Charter school impact: $7.2 million in FY25 in tuition and lost state aid. - Discussion of selling former school buildings (Barrows, Waterman) to generate $750,000 one-time for capital needs, but that will not be available in future years. The city solicitor clarified the funds are intended for capital improvements, not tuition. #### Fire Department Budget (Chief, Director Strom) - Proposed overtime budget: $6.3 million (up slightly from FY25 actual of $6.073 million). The chief noted summer overtime is highest and 12 firefighters short, with vacancies due to contractual limits. Fuel costs are a concern due to global prices. - There are 15 firefighters on occupational injury; seven are waiting for state pension board decisions. These injuries increase overtime. - The department had to cut vehicle replacements; two staff vehicles are included. - Council members expressed concern about accuracy of overtime projections given prior years' underfunding. #### Fire Alarm Department - Budget increased for computer maintenance and repairs (licenses increasing). No significant questions. #### Canvassing Department (Director Lima via video) - Proposed operating budget for elections: $215,000, the lowest since 2018. Savings achieved by reducing poll workers (from 315 to 270), cutting poll worker management software (delayed until federal funds available), and benefits from moving the primary to Wednesday (saving ~$25,000). - The department faces increased voter registration transactions (23,822 in 2025) and security needs. Federal election security grant ($50,000) has been fully spent on physical security upgrades. - Potential new state Voting Rights Act may require bilingual ballots, increasing costs. Director Lima noted that federal executive orders could impact mail ballot processing. #### Law Department (Solicitor) - Running under budget at 72.8% year-to-date. No provision for lawsuit settlements; the solicitor recommended budgeting a small contingency. Outside legal services are used for specialized cases and are negotiated at municipal rates (~$200/hour). #### Executive Office (Director Moretti) - Proposing a 0.75% increase (less than 1%), achieved by eliminating one administrative position and consolidating government affairs with communications. Compensation increases for 18 administrative appointees (totaling ~$45,000) were included, but the mayor offered to forego those raises if the council desires, reallocating funds to police vehicles. - The mayor receives a $3,000 annual expense stipend (not monthly). Four city vehicles are assigned to executive staff; fuel and maintenance are charged to the police budget—a legacy accounting practice. Council members questioned this and requested transparency. ### Key Outcomes - No final votes on the budget were taken. The committee will continue deliberations in subsequent hearings, including a planned executive session regarding police contract negotiations. - The council president noted that a 7.44% tax levy increase would require seven out of nine votes (four-fifths) per the city charter, and that nothing is finalized. - The council extended the meeting twice by 30-minute increments to allow full discussion. - Public comment was invited at the meeting's start and end; no online participants spoke. - The meeting adjourned at 11:49 PM.

results.title: 449 Stealing America: Indigenous Slavery and the American Revolution
results.creator: YORK UNITED METHODIST CHURCH
results.description: More than half a million Indigenous people were enslaved within the present-day borders of the United States. Historian Linford Fisher spent fifteen years in archives across North America, the Caribbean, and Britain to investigate this forgotten history. What he found was not a second story running alongside African slavery. It was something different in kind. Europeans and early Americans enslaved people who lived on land they intended to possess. This practice made slavery a tool of dispossession. The American Revolution is where this process accelerated. Lin and Lorén Spears, a Narragansett tribal citizen and the executive director of the Tomaquag Museum , trace how the Revolution opened space for captive raiding on the western frontier, how Native nations weighed which side to take during the war, and how their Stolen Relations digital project is recovering the names of the Natives early Americans enslaved. results.description: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Director Rohit Chopra testified on a semi-annual report of his agency before the House Financial Services Committee. Several members of the Republican majority asked Mr. Chopra about concerns of privacy and expenses relating to Section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act, which requires financial institutions to report certain data on credit applications for small businesses owned by women and minorities. Other topics included the CFPB's work on combating junk fees and predatory lending, and a proposed rule to subject large nonbank companies that offer financial services, such as Apple and Google, to the same regulatory oversight as banks. At the time of this event, the Supreme Court was considering a case about the CFPB's funding structure; it is an independent agency within the Federal Reserve and not funded by Congress. This is the first part of the program. Sponsor: House Financial Services Committee

results.title: East Providence City Council Meeting - July 7, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # East Providence City Council Meeting - July 7, 2026 This regular meeting of the East Providence City Council covered a range of topics including sewer abatements, proclamations, a public hearing and final passage of an ordinance appropriating $340,035 for softball field improvements, approvals of licenses, communications from the SBA, and various council member items regarding infrastructure, public safety, and community events. The meeting concluded with several resolutions and adjournment. ### Consent Calendar - **Sewer Charge Abatement:** Approved $378.58 abatement for a water break related to a bathroom pipe, recommended by the Department of Public Works. Motion by Councilman Bogarty, seconded by Councilman Lawson. Unanimous. - **Consent Calendar Items:** Council journals (June 16, 2026), new addresses (156 Amarillo St, 9 Regent Drive), cancellations and abatements ($6,647.24). Motion by Councilwoman Sousa, seconded by Councilman Fogerty. Unanimous. - **Licenses:** Bundled items 1-10 (entertainment, alcohol, new business licenses for East Providence Fuel, etc.) approved with a motion by Councilman Lawson and second by Councilwoman Sousa. Unanimous. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **Softball Field Improvements (Public Hearing):** Multiple speakers expressed support for lighting and improvements at Amaral Field. - Richard Hogan (President of East Providence Central Little League) detailed the league's growth (200-250 players, 80 volunteers), the lack of lights causing scheduling difficulties, and the need for equity with baseball fields. He noted that the junior/senior division girls will represent Rhode Island in Pennsylvania. - Christina O'Reilly (coach and parent) explained that without lights, older girls (13-15) cannot practice after school, limiting seasons. She cited a Women's Sports Foundation study that girls drop out at twice the rate of boys by age 14. - Jonathan McGowan (Vice President of East Providence Central Little League) highlighted the growth from 76 players to nearly 100 in one year and urged support. - A resident (parent of six, five girls) spoke in favor, showing the growth in divisions (coach pitch, minors, majors, juniors/seniors) and the team's success in all-stars. - **Additional Hours for Fuel Sales (Public Hearing):** No public speakers for or against. The applicant (Nicholas Lambrose, attorney) explained the need for 24-hour fuel sales at the new East Providence Fuels (formerly Exxon). The council clarified that during 1 a.m. to 6 a.m., only fuel sales would occur, not repairs. Approved with that condition. ### Discussion Items - **Council President Rodrigues - World Cup Recognition:** Rodrigues thanked the Scottish "Tartan Army" for their positive impact, including a $10,000 donation to Hasbro Children's Hospital and general goodwill. He wore a kilt in tribute. - **Councilman Lawson - Budget Requests:** Proposed adding a DPW rodent/pest control specialist (like Cranston and Warwick), improvements to Oldham (city-owned building), and reviewing school department head teaching loads. The administration acknowledged and will consider. - **Councilman Lawson - Parking for Crescent Park Events:** With construction reducing parking, he suggested shuttles from off-site lots, local traffic restrictions, and using private lots. Councilwoman Sousa noted that a shuttle was used for the recent block party and should be replicated. The administration will coordinate. - **Councilman Lawson - Willet Avenue Traffic Redesign:** He criticized the road diet and yield sign configuration, stating residents feel ignored. Administration explained the redesign was based on resident feedback and engineering standards to reduce speeding, with no major accidents reported. Lawson disagreed, calling the road diet unsafe. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Veterans Hero Banners:** Out of 108 orders, 86 paid; banners have been ordered and will be installed by August on Roger Williams Ave, Bullocks Point Ave, and Pawtucket Ave (pending confirmation). A digital payment option will be implemented for future orders. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Pedestrian Crosswalks on Warren Avenue:** Asked for timeline on crosswalk signals at Lions Ave and 7th St. Administration will check with DPW director Dan. Sousa stressed safety issues for children crossing to bus stops. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Speed Monitoring on Burgess Avenue:** Requested traffic study and calming measures. Council Vice President Rigo recommended contacting police chief for a traffic study first. Administration will request study from chief. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Street Light Adjustment:** Requested brighter lighting in dark neighborhoods, especially near parks. Administration noted balance between safety, energy cost, and bulb life, and will review specific locations. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Trash Receptacles at Parks and Bus Stops:** Requested more trash cans at parks (e.g., Martello Park) and bus stops. Administration stated RIPTA is responsible for bus stops, but will coordinate; they noted a carry-in/carry-out policy and capacity limits for 44 parks. - **Council Vice President Rigo - ADU Tax Stabilization:** Second passage of ordinance amending tax stabilization for qualified businesses to include accessory dwelling units (ADUs), for owner-occupied properties with homestead exemption only. Rigo explained it helps with housing crisis without building on new land. Passed 4-1. - **Resolutions:** - **Window Replacement at City Hall:** Contract with Red Oak Remodeling for $482,545 for exterior windows, previously discussed. Unanimous. - **Easement for Police Substation:** Granting easement to Narragansett Electric for power to police substation at Pierce Field, previously discussed. Unanimous. - **Furniture for Community Center:** Authorizing purchase of furniture, fixtures, and equipment from W.B. Mason for $172,539.75, using previously allocated funds (ARPA/CPF grant). Unanimous. ### Key Outcomes - **Sewer Abatement Approved** Unanimous. - **Consent Calendar and Licenses Approved** Unanimous. - **Pierce Softball Field Improvements Ordinance Approved** Unanimously (second passage, public hearing held). The $340,035 allocation covers lights, paved parking, walkways, guardrails, and will be contracted with New School Lighting. - **Additional Hours for Fuel Sales Approved** (with condition of no repairs between 1 a.m. and 6 a.m.) Unanimous. - **ADU Tax Stabilization Ordinance Approved** 4-1. - **Resolutions for City Hall Windows, Easement, and Community Center Furniture Approved** Unanimously. - **Veterans Hero Banners:** Expected installation by August. - **Willet Avenue Traffic Pattern:** Administration stands by redesign; further complaints will be brought back. - **Various Council Requests:** Administration will follow up on parking, speed monitoring, crosswalks, street lights, and trash receptacles.

results.title: THE CHRONICLES OF AMERICA " THE PURITANS " JOHN WINTHROP 1924 YALE UNIVERSITY (SILENT FILM) 10424
results.creator: PeriscopeFilm
results.description: In 1923 the Yale University Press commissioned films based on the fifty volumes in their "Chronicles of America" book series. Ultimately, only fifteen episodes were produced. This film from 1924 is entitled "The Puritans". According to the book "Hollywood on the Hudson", Yale spent $1.25 million dollars making the films and then found it could not easily recoup the investment, because the films were not theatrically viable and most schools in that era did not have appropriate infrastructure or the experience using films to teach. However, Chronicles of America persisted for many years and was the first documentary series shown on television in 1941 when it aired on pioneering station WNBT.   The film was adapted by Evangeline W. Andrews and directed by the Film Guild's Frank Tuttle, who went on to sign with Paramount.   The cast includes Arthur Hohl as John Winthrop, Audrey Hart as Margaret Winthrop, Henry Van Bousen and Roger Williams , Allan Brander as Thomas Dudley, Osgood Perkins as Thomas Morton and Royal B. Tracy as Archbishop Laud.     The film attempts to tell the story of the early days of the Puritan settlements in New England, with dueling attempts to lead the colonists by John Winthrop and Thomas Morton, and intrigue in England involving an alleged violation of the Puritan Charter. This conflict pitted the avowed enemy of the Puritans Archibishop Laud and the "father of American colonization" and founder of Maine, Sir Ferdinando Gorges. Other subplots in the film include Roger Williams' belief that the Charter is unlawful because it will shortchange the Native Americans. (A study guide is really needed to fully understand the film, and this was one of the problems it faced upon release as the only guide that apparently existed was the book it was based upon.)   John Winthrop was an English Puritan lawyer and one of the leading figures in founding the Massachusetts Bay Colony. This was the second major settlement in New England following Plymouth Colony. Winthrop led the first large wave of colonizers from England in 1630 and served as governor for 12 of the colony's first 20 years. His writings and vision of the colony as a Puritan "city upon a hill" dominated New England colonial development, influencing the governments and religions of neighboring colonies. The film also shows Thomas Morton a colonist in North America from Devon, England. A lawyer, writer and social reformer, he was famed for founding the British colony of Merrymount, located in what is now Quincy, Massachusetts, and for his work in studying Native American culture.   Chronicles of America is the title of a fifty volume series of books on American history. Originally printed in 1918, the volumes were written by historians of the time about various aspects of American History. The series was edited by Allen Johnson and published by Yale University.In 1923, Yale decided to create a series of films based on the books. Fifteen films were ultimately produced.   We encourage viewers to add comments and, especially, to provide additional information about our videos by adding a comment!   See something interesting?   Tell people what it is and what they can see by writing something for example: "01:00:12:00 -- President Roosevelt is seen meeting with Winston Churchill at the Quebec Conference."   This film is part of the Periscope Film LLC archive, one of the largest historic military, transportation, and aviation stock footage collections in the USA. Entirely film backed, this material is available for licensing in 24p HD, 2k and 4k. For more information visit http://www.PeriscopeFilm.com
